lead: A fixed headlamp points where the car points. On a bend the beam goes straight on and the inside of the curve stays dark; with a loaded boot the nose lifts and the dipped beam climbs into oncoming eyes. An adaptive front lighting system (AFS) moves or reshapes the beam instead: a swivel motor turns the lamp with the steering, a levelling motor tilts it to hold the cut-off on the road, and the ECU picks a beam pattern to suit the road. Only a few universities teach this topic.
prereq: You need: the dipped-beam cut-off from front, rear, interior and special-purpose lighting.

blocks.text: Levelling is rotation about a horizontal axis (pitch). Passengers in the back and a full boot push the rear down and tilt the whole body nose-up; braking dive and acceleration squat do the same briefly. The level motor tilts the lamp down by the same angle so the cut-off stays where it was set. Headlamp aim is given as a slope: an aim of −1% means the cut-off falls 10 cm for every 10 m ahead. Lamps with a very bright dipped beam, such as xenon HID, must have automatic levelling and headlamp cleaning by law.

Swivel, or dynamic bending light, is rotation about a vertical axis (yaw). The lamp turns into the bend with the steering, typically up to about 15° each way, so the beam lights the road the car is about to use. Static cornering light is a separate lamp, or an extra LED segment, that switches on at low speed when the indicator is on or the steering is turned hard, lighting the side of a junction.

Many AFS lamps also change the beam pattern with speed: a wide, short town light; the normal country light; a longer, slightly raised motorway light at high speed; and an adverse-weather light that cuts light just ahead of the car, where wet roads glare back.

The AFS ECU reads the steering angle sensor (wheel angle and rate), the vehicle speed sent over the CAN bus by the ABS ECU from its wheel-speed sensors, front and rear ride-height sensors (the difference gives pitch) and, on newer cars, a forward camera that sees oncoming and leading vehicles.

It computes target swivel and pitch angles and commands two small motors per lamp. A stepper motor moves in fixed steps and the ECU counts them from a reference stop; a DC motor carries a position sensor, often a potentiometer, so the ECU can close the loop. The swivel command shrinks with speed: large at junction speed, small on the highway, and it saturates at its limit so the beam never sweeps across the centre line. On a fault the lamps park straight ahead and slightly low, so the driver keeps a legal dipped beam.

blocks.where: θ is the pitch angle of the body, Δh the drop of the rear axle in metres with the front axle at its normal height, and b the wheelbase in metres. Every point of the body, including the lamp, tilts by the same θ.

blocks.text: A matrix headlamp builds the high beam from many LED segments. The camera finds other vehicles and the ECU switches off only the segments aimed at them, keeping high beam everywhere else. This function is called adaptive driving beam (ADB); matrix LED is one way to build it.

examples.question: A car with a wheelbase of 2.5 m has its headlamps aimed at −1.0%. Loading the boot lowers the rear axle by 20 mm while the front stays put. (a) Find the pitch angle. (b) Find the new aim and how far the cut-off rises at 25 m. (c) The swivel command is 0.15 × steering-wheel angle, capped at 15°. Find the swivel for steering-wheel angles of 90° and 120°.
steps: The nose tilts up by 0.46°, which is a slope of 0.008 = 0.8%. The aim goes from −1.0% to −1.0 + 0.8 = −0.2%: the beam now falls only 2 cm per 10 m.
At 25 m the cut-off rises by 25 × 0.008 = 0.20 m. The level motor must tilt the lamp down by 0.46° to bring the aim back to −1.0%.
At 90°: 0.15 × 90° = 13.5°, below the cap, so the lamp turns 13.5°.
At 120°: 0.15 × 120° = 18° is above the cap, so the command saturates at 15°.
examples.answer: (a) 0.46°. (b) The aim becomes −0.2% and the cut-off rises 0.20 m at 25 m, so the level motor tilts the lamp 0.46° down. (c) 13.5° at 90°; 15° (capped) at 120°.

traps: Levelling corrects pitch (up and down) for load; swivel corrects yaw (left and right) for steering. A car can have one without the other.
Using the distance from the rear axle to the lamp in the pitch angle. The body turns about the front axle, so use the wheelbase; the lamp's position does not change the angle.
Getting the direction wrong: a sinking rear tilts the beam up, so the motor tilts the lamp down.
Check which angle a swivel gain is defined on. If it is given per degree of road-wheel angle, divide the steering-wheel angle by the steering ratio first.
Ignoring the cap: beyond about 15° more steering gives no more swivel.

quiz.q: Which motor corrects pitch, and for what?
quiz.a: The levelling motor; it tilts the lamp to hold the cut-off on the road when load, braking or acceleration tilts the body.

quiz.q: Name four inputs to the AFS ECU.
quiz.a: Steering angle, vehicle speed (from the ABS ECU over CAN), front and rear ride height, and the forward camera.

quiz.q: Why is swivel limited to about 15°?
quiz.a: Beyond that the beam would sweep across the centre line into oncoming drivers, so the command saturates.

quiz.q: State the difference between dynamic bending light, static cornering light and adaptive driving beam.
quiz.a: Dynamic bending light swivels the main lamp with the steering. Static cornering light switches on an extra lamp or segment at low speed to light the side of a junction. Adaptive driving beam keeps the high beam on and blanks only the parts aimed at other vehicles.

quiz.q: The steering-wheel angle is 60°, the steering ratio is 15:1 and the swivel gain is 2.0° per degree of road-wheel angle, capped at 15°. Find the swivel.
quiz.a: Road-wheel angle = 60 ÷ 15 = 4°. Swivel = 2.0 × 4° = 8°, below the 15° cap.

quiz.q: The rear of a car with a 2.5 m wheelbase drops 30 mm. Find the pitch angle and the rise of the cut-off at 20 m.
The camera of a matrix-LED car fails. What should the lamps do, and why?
quiz.a: Fall back to the normal dipped beam with swivel parked straight ahead, and light a warning: without the camera the ECU cannot see other road users, so it cannot promise that the high beam will not dazzle them.

beyond: Pixel headlamps with thousands of switchable points, made with micro-mirror chips or micro-LED arrays, can draw a dark box round each road user and even project symbols on the road. The camera is now shared with lane keeping and emergency braking on a domain controller. Search terms: adaptive driving beam, pixel headlamp, dynamic bending light.

figure.caption: A 20 mm drop at the rear tilts the whole body 0.46° about the front axle, lifting the cut-off 0.20 m at 25 m; the level motor tilts the lamp back down. Seen from above, the swivel turns the beam 13.5° for 90° of steering and stops at 15°.
